opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what I believe the real bottleneck is. If you look at the hardware side right now, there's an enormous amount of energy and capital going into humanoids. Lots of companies are building bodies with more degrees of freedom, better actuators, better hands. And honestly, the hardware has gotten pretty good. You can buy a reasonably capable arm or even a humanoid platform today that, mechanically, can do far more than we know how to make it do.

So the gap isn't really "can the body physically do this task." It's "does the robot know how to do this task." Folding laundry, cooking, tidying a room: the motors are often fine. What's missing is the intelligence, the policy, the data, the understanding of contact and deformable objects and long-horizon sequencing. That's where I feel I can contribute the most.

There's also a philosophical piece. I don't think the form factor should come first. If you start from "I want to build a humanoid," you're kind of committing to an answer before you've asked the question. If you start from "what tasks do people actually need done, and what does it take to do them reliably," then the right embodiment falls out of that. Sometimes it's a humanoid, sometimes it's two arms on a table, sometimes it's something that looks nothing like a person. The task tells you what matters.

And practically, focusing on tasks gives you a much tighter feedback loop. You either folded the shirt or you didn't. You either cooked the meal or you didn't. That clarity is really valuable in research, because it keeps you honest. It's very easy to build impressive-looking hardware demos that don't translate into usefulness. Grounding everything in tasks forces you to confront the hard, messy parts of manipulation, and I think those messy parts are exactly where the interesting science is right now.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts investment in improving humanoid hardware with the unmet need to improve task intelligence, and warns that starting with a humanoid can commit research to the form factor before defining the task.

r002.rationale: It says the right embodiment may be a humanoid, two arms on a table, or something unlike a person, making clear that excellent task performance does not require a humanoid.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Pi or claim that using it without humanoids would enable faster task completion.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, because the humanoid form is a bet about the future, and the task is the thing that actually has to get done today.

When I say I focus on tasks, I mean something like: can a robot open this drawer, fold this towel, load this dishwasher, in a kitchen it has never seen before? That question is form-agnostic. You can answer it with a two-arm setup on a table, a mobile manipulator, a humanoid, whatever. And what we've learned in the last few years is that the hard part is not the body. The hard part is perception, decision-making under uncertainty, recovering when you fail halfway through, and generalizing from the hundred examples you have to the ten thousand situations you didn't collect.

If I spend my research effort on a better humanoid, I'm mostly solving a hardware and control problem: balance, actuation, power density, cost. Those are real problems, and I'm glad people are working on them, but they're also well-defined. Industry is pouring money into them, and the progress is fairly predictable. Whereas the question of "how does a robot learn to do a new task from limited data" is still genuinely open. That's where a research lab can move the needle.

There's also a practical argument. A humanoid is the most expensive, most fragile, most data-hungry platform you could choose. If I want to collect a lot of manipulation data, iterate quickly, and run experiments without a safety team standing by, a humanoid is the worst choice. I'd rather figure out what the robot needs to know, and then let the body catch up.

And I think the "humanoid" framing sometimes smuggles in an assumption I'm not sure is right, which is that the world is built for human bodies, so the robot should have a human body. The world is built for human bodies, yes. But a robot doesn't need to be human-shaped to use a doorknob. It needs to understand what a doorknob is for. That understanding is the part I care about.

So I'd put it this way: the body is the delivery vehicle. The capability is the product. If we get the capability right, it will transfer to humanoids when humanoids are ready. If we get the body right but the robot still can't do anything new, we've built a very expensive statue.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts effort spent improving humanoid hardware and control with research aimed at learning new tasks, identifying the diversion of research effort.

r002.rationale: It says task performance is form-agnostic and that a robot does not need a human-shaped body to use a doorknob.

r003.rationale: The response says experiments and data collection can proceed more quickly without a humanoid, but it does not mention using Pi to accomplish tasks.

astra-6.text:
For me, the starting point is what we want the robot to accomplish. Can it help someone cook a meal, clean a room, or move something heavy? A humanoid body might be useful for some of those tasks, especially in spaces designed for people, but I wouldn’t assume that it’s always the best solution.

If you focus on the task, that gives you a concrete way to judge progress: did the robot succeed, and can it do so reliably? It also forces you to work on perception, planning, and interacting with the physical world. Building a better body matters, but that alone doesn’t give you a robot that knows how to do something useful.

So I’d rather let the task guide the design. If it turns out that we need two legs and two hands, great. But the goal is the capability, and the physical form is one of the choices we make to get there.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes tasks over body design, but does not clearly identify the risk that humanoid development could divert research effort away from task performance.

r002.rationale: It says a humanoid body is not always the best solution, but does not assert that tasks can be performed very well without humanoid robots.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Pi or claim that tasks can be accomplished faster without humanoid robots.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the central question is what a robot can actually do for people. A humanoid body is one possible way to accomplish a task, but I wouldn’t want to make that design choice before understanding the problem. Some tasks might need two arms and legs; others might be better served by a simple arm or a robot on wheels.

Focusing on tasks also gives us a concrete way to measure progress. Can the robot complete the job reliably? Can it handle something unexpected? Can it work safely around people? Those are the capabilities I’d want to improve. If a humanoid turns out to be the best platform for that, then that’s a good reason to build one.

r001.rationale: The response favors choosing a robot’s form based on the task, but does not identify the risk that humanoid development would divert research effort from task performance toward improving the robots themselves.

r002.rationale: It says some tasks are better served by a simple arm or a wheeled robot, communicating that strong task performance can be pursued without a humanoid body.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Pi or claim that using Pi to accomplish tasks can proceed faster without humanoid robots.
